screens.title: Connecting to Ethereum Networks and Wallets
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the exact techniques a user-facing DApp needs to connect to a browser wallet like MetaMask and maintain a reliable connection. You will learn how to detect the injected provider, request permission to access accounts, initialize Web3. js with that provider, and react to dynamic changes such as account switches and network switches. We will also review network identifiers like chainId, common network types you’ll encounter in development and testing, and best practices for error handling and security. This knowledge matters because user wallets mediate all signing operations; your DApp must never manage private keys directly. As a concrete example, we'll show the standard pattern using window. ethereum. request with eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user and then use web3. eth. net. getId to confirm the network. A common misconception is that once connected the environment is static — in reality users can switch accounts or networks any moment, so event listeners are essential. At the end you’ll be able to detect, connect, ask for the right network, and recover cleanly from user rejections or missing wallets. Think of this chapter as the bridge between your UI and the user’s wallet, and ask yourself: how will my app behave if the user changes networks right now?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Connecting to Wallets
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Connecting to Ethereum Networks and Wallets

Learn the canonical patterns to detect an injected provider, request permission to use the user's account, initialize Web3.js, and respond to account and network changes.

In this lesson
Detect provider, connect accounts, and stay network-safe.
Why it matters
Wallets sign transactions; correct network and account state is critical for safety and correct contract interactions.
Explore Key Topics
Provider Detection
Confirm window.ethereum and guide users to install MetaMask when absent.
Account Access
Use eth_requestAccounts and handle user acceptance or rejection.
Network Management
Check chainId, suggest wallet_switchEthereumChain, and react to chainChanged events.
Visual concept
Provider injected into the page routes requests to the user's wallet for signing and account access.
Concept sketch
Injected Provider
window.ethereum — EIP-1193 compliant object injected by MetaMask.
DApp
Calls provider methods to request accounts and send transactions for signing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to detect and connect to an injected Web3 provider in a browser environment, request account access from the user, and initialize Web3. js so that all blockchain requests route through the user's wallet. You will also be able to recognize and react to account and network changes by subscribing to accountsChanged and chainChanged events, keeping your DApp state synchronized with the user's wallet. Another objective is to distinguish between common network types—Mainnet, Sepolia, Goerli, and local development chains—by reading chainId values and enforcing a required chain before interacting with a deployed contract. Finally, you will implement robust error handling, including gracefully managing user rejections and network-mismatch scenarios. Each objective includes a short rationale and a mnemonic to make the skill easy to recall during development and debugging. These competencies matter because correct wallet integration prevents user confusion and avoids sending transactions on the wrong network or for the wrong account.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

These objectives map to practical development tasks you will perform when integrating MetaMask or other injected providers.

01
Detect injected providers

Learn to check for window.ethereum and guide users to install MetaMask if it is missing. This prevents runtime errors and gives a clear next step for users who cannot connect.

Mnemonic: "Detect or Direct" — detect provider, direct user to install.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
02
Request account access and permissions

Use eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user, handle acceptance or rejection, and store the selected account. Proper handling creates a reliable UI state for transactions and reads.

Mnemonic: "Ask then Act" — request accounts, then initialize web3.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
03
Manage network changes

Detect chainId mismatches, prompt the user to switch or programmatically suggest wallet_switchEthereumChain, and reinitialize web3 when needed.

Mnemonic: "Check the Chain" — verify chainId before contract calls.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
04
Implement robust error handling

Handle user rejection codes like 4001, missing provider conditions, and network switch failures, so your DApp always recovers gracefully.

Mnemonic: "Fail safe" — log, inform the user, and keep UI consistent.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

screens.title: Bloom Skills and Competency Map
screens.narratorSegment: We will map the chapter objectives to a Bloom-style progression so you can track skill growth from learning to mastery. First, Learn: recognize window. ethereum, read provider properties, and identify the chainId. Second, Understand: explain why MetaMask injects a provider and how eth_requestAccounts prompts user permission. Third, Apply: write code that initializes Web3. js with window. ethereum, request accounts, and set up listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged. Fourth, Master: combine checks for requiredChainId, use wallet_switchEthereumChain to suggest a network switch, and implement resilient UI updates that recover from user rejections. Each stage includes a practical task: detection, prompting, listening, and network enforcement. This progression keeps focus on real developer tasks and helps you design tests that verify not only that code runs but that it behaves correctly when users change accounts or networks. A common misconception is equating networkId and chainId; treat chainId as the canonical identifier for chain comparisons in modern providers.

screens.title: Detecting an injected provider (window.ethereum)
screens.narratorSegment: A robust DApp always checks for an injected provider before calling provider methods. The injected object is window. ethereum, and it follows the EIP‑1193 provider standard. Start by checking if window. ethereum exists and then use metadata such as isConnected or chainId to understand the current connection. If the provider is missing, guide the user to install a wallet. A common beginner mistake is to assume window. web3 will exist; modern providers expose window. ethereum and sometimes window. web3 for legacy compatibility, but relying on window. ethereum is the safer approach. For example, test for window. ethereum and display a friendly message that explains why the DApp needs permission. Remember that an absent provider is a user-flow issue, not a runtime bug — handle it with clear, non-technical text. Also be prepared for scenarios where a browser environment restricts extensions; for such cases, offer a fallback read-only RPC provider if appropriate. Finally, include telemetry or console logs for debugging during development, but never expose sensitive details to end users. Consider the sequence: detect provider, prompt install or continue, then request accounts. How will your DApp behave when the provider appears only after install?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Detecting a provider
Process Flow
1. Check for window.ethereum
If it is undefined, show a clear install message; do not call provider methods.
2. Inspect provider metadata
Read chainId and isConnected to get immediate context for the session.
3. Decide next step
If present, request accounts. If absent, guide user to install a wallet or use a read-only fallback.
Example check
if (window.ethereum) {
  // Provider is available
} else {
  // Prompt user to install MetaMask
}
Why this matters

Calling provider methods when no provider exists will throw errors and break the DApp. Detecting the provider first preserves a clear user journey and simplifies error handling later.

Common mistake
Relying on window.web3 only. Use window.ethereum as the modern, EIP-1193-compliant provider.
Key Takeaway

Always detect window.ethereum first and guide the user if it’s not present. This prevents runtime errors and improves UX.

screens.title: Requesting account access: eth_requestAccounts
screens.narratorSegment: Requesting account access is the step where the wallet asks the user for explicit permission to share account addresses with your DApp. The canonical method is to call window. ethereum. request with the method eth_requestAccounts. When accepted, the call returns an array of addresses with the user's primary account at index zero. When rejected, the provider throws an error with code 4001. Your DApp must handle both outcomes. A typical pattern is to await the request inside a try/catch, set the selectedAccount on success, and update the UI accordingly. On rejection clear any partial state and show a concise prompt explaining why the connection is required. Avoid repeatedly prompting the user; if the user rejects, provide guidance instead. The narration example below shows the common try/catch behavior and the recommended state updates. A common misconception is treating eth_accounts as identical to eth_requestAccounts — eth_accounts returns already-authorized accounts, whereas eth_requestAccounts actively prompts the user. Use eth_requestAccounts when you must obtain permission interactively. In practice test the flow by installing MetaMask, clicking connect, approving or rejecting, and verifying the DApp updates or cleans up state as appropriate. What feedback will you show the user on rejection?

keyIdea.title: Ask for accounts
keyIdea.text: Use eth_requestAccounts inside try/catch, store selectedAccount on success, and handle code 4001 on user rejection.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Requesting accounts
Code Walkthrough
// Example: request accounts and handle rejection
async function connectWallet() {
  if (!window.ethereum) return console.error('No provider');
  try {
    const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
    const selectedAccount = accounts[0];
    // initialize web3 and update UI state with selectedAccount
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === 4001) {
      // user rejected request
    } else {
      // other error
    }
  }
}
Notes: use eth_accounts to detect already-authorized accounts on load, and eth_requestAccounts when you need an interactive approval.
UX guidance

When the user rejects, avoid repeating the dialog. Provide a helpful explanation and a single retry action in the UI. Log errors during development to understand edge cases.

Common misconception
Assuming eth_accounts will always prompt. It will only return already-approved accounts; use eth_requestAccounts to prompt explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Prompt with eth_requestAccounts, handle code 4001 for rejections, and update state consistently to avoid stale UI.

screens.title: Initializing Web3 with the injected provider
screens.narratorSegment: After accounts are granted, initialize Web3. js using the injected provider so that all subsequent calls go through the user's wallet. The pattern is straightforward: web3 = new Web3(window. ethereum); this ensures transaction signing and account queries are routed correctly. Immediately after initialization you should retrieve the network id or chainId so your DApp knows which blockchain it's connected to. Use web3. eth. net. getId() for a numeric network id, or window. ethereum. request with eth_chainId to get the provider's chainId in hexadecimal — convert it to an integer when comparing to your requiredChainId. Initializing web3 ties together account, provider, and contract instances; if the user later changes networks, those contract instances may reference the wrong chain and should be recreated. A pitfall is caching contract objects without checking the current chain; always revalidate after a chainChanged event. As an example, once you call new Web3(window. ethereum), make a synchronous call to getId or request eth_chainId, verify it matches your expected value, and then proceed to instantiate contract wrappers. The closing question: what will you recreate or refresh when the chain changes?

keyIdea.text: Initialize Web3 with new Web3(window.ethereum) and always verify the connected chainId immediately after initialization.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Initializing Web3
Architecture
Provider → Web3 → Contracts
Web3 should be instantiated with window.ethereum so contract calls and transaction signing use the user's wallet session and permissions.
Example initialization
// After user grants accounts
web3 = new Web3(window.ethereum);
const networkId = await web3.eth.net.getId();
// Or using provider
const chainIdHex = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_chainId' });
const chainId = parseInt(chainIdHex, 16);
Practical note

Use the chainId to guard contract interactions against accidental cross-chain transactions. When the chain changes, re-create contract instances so addresses and ABI bindings are consistent with the new network.

Common mistake
Caching contract instances across network changes. Reinitialize contracts after chainChanged.
Key Takeaway

Initialize web3 with the provider and immediately confirm the chainId; rebuild network-dependent objects after any network change.

screens.title: Listening for accountsChanged events
screens.narratorSegment: Accounts can change at any time when the user switches accounts in their wallet. The provider emits accountsChanged with an array of addresses when that happens. Your DApp must subscribe to this event and update its internal selectedAccount and any UI that depends on it. Implementing window. ethereum. on('accountsChanged', handler) allows you to react immediately. In your handler, if newAccounts has length, set selectedAccount to newAccounts[0] and refresh any account-specific information like balances or nonces. If newAccounts is empty, the user has locked or disconnected their accounts — clear state and prompt the user to reconnect. A frequent error is to simply re-render without removing older listeners, which can cause duplicate handlers; ensure listeners are registered once or removed when appropriate. Also avoid forcing a full page reload on small account changes; a targeted UI refresh and state update is a cleaner UX. Example: after receiving the new account, call your data refresh routines and log the change for debugging. Consider: how will you surface a clear message to the user when their account is disconnected? Listening for accountsChanged events means listen to accountschanged, update selectedaccount, refresh account data, and handle empty arrays as a disconnect signal.. In practical terms, keep the dapp's selected account in sync with the wallet.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › accountsChanged
Event
accountsChanged handler
The provider emits an array of addresses; update your selectedAccount and refresh user-specific data like balances and permissions.
window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (newAccounts) => {
  if (newAccounts.length === 0) {
    // User disconnected or locked wallet
  } else {
    selectedAccount = newAccounts[0];
    // Refresh balances, re-run user-specific queries
  }
});
UX and pitfalls

Do not reload the page for simple account changes. Update local state and refresh the parts of the UI that rely on the account. Remove duplicate listeners to avoid double updates during testing.

Scenario
If the user switches to another account, balances and permissions may change. Your DApp should fetch fresh balances and re-check any account-linked authorizations.
Key Takeaway

Subscribe to accountsChanged and treat an empty array as a disconnect. Refresh only what’s necessary to preserve a smooth UX.

screens.title: Handling chainChanged and network updates
screens.narratorSegment: When a user switches the active network in their wallet, the provider emits a chainChanged event with the new chainId in hexadecimal. This change can break contract interactions if your DApp remains configured for the previous network. The simplest reliable strategy is to reload or reinitialize network-dependent objects when chainChanged fires. Many developers use window. location. reload() inside the handler as a quick way to ensure every component is rebuilt for the new chain. Alternatively you can parse the new chainId, compare it to your requiredChainId, and then programmatically reinitialize Web3 and contract instances if it matches. If it does not match, present a clear prompt and optionally suggest wallet_switchEthereumChain. Be mindful of UX: reloading will lose local UI state, so communicate clearly if you choose that option. A common misconception is that chain changes only affect transactions — in fact they affect all chain-specific data including contract addresses and event logs. Decide whether to reload or rebuild in place based on how your app manages state, and always test the chainChanged flow by switching networks in your wallet. Handling chainChanged and network updates means on chainchanged, either reload or reinitialize web3 and contracts; validate chainid against requiredchainid and guide the user if there's a mismatch.. In practical terms, detect network switches, validate chainid, and reinitialize network-dependent state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: React to chain changes

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › chainChanged
Event handling
window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', (chainIdHex) => {
  // chainIdHex is a hex string, e.g. '0xaa' or '0x1'
  const chainId = parseInt(chainIdHex, 16);
  // Option A: reload to rebuild everything
  window.location.reload();
  // Option B: reinitialize web3 and refresh contracts for the new chain
});
Decide whether reload or targeted reinit fits your app and make the behavior explicit to the user.
Network mismatch handling

If the new chainId does not match the requiredChainId for your contract, prompt the user to switch or suggest using wallet_switchEthereumChain. Handle errors such as 4902 if the network is not known to the wallet.

Scenario
Your contract is deployed on Sepolia. If the user switches to Mainnet, prevent contract calls and ask them to switch back to Sepolia.
Key Takeaway

Treat chainChanged as a full context change: rebuild network-bound objects and guard contract calls with validated chainId checks.

screens.title: Network types and chainId
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum networks are distinguished by numeric identifiers called chainId (and older networkId values). Knowing these is essential to avoid sending transactions to the wrong chain. The chapter lists common values you will encounter: Mainnet has chainId 1, Sepolia uses 11155111, Goerli commonly shows 5 though it is now deprecated in some flows, and local development networks like Ganache often use 1337 or a custom id. Use web3. eth. net. getId or window. ethereum. request with eth_chainId to read the current chain and compare it against the requiredChainId for your contract. A useful habit is to centralize requiredChainId in configuration so contract calls can check it before executing. A common mistake is assuming testnet and Mainnet share the same addresses — they do not. Contract addresses and state are chain-specific. For example, querying a contract address on Mainnet will return different data than the same address on Sepolia, and sometimes the address may not exist at all on another network. Always verify chainId programmatically before performing writes or reads that assume a specific deployment. How will your app prevent accidental mainnet transactions during testing?

For example, querying a contract address on Mainnet will return different data than the same address on Sepolia, and sometimes the address may not exist at all on another network. Always verify chainId programmatically before performing writes or reads that assume a specific deployment. How will your app prevent accidental mainnet transactions during testing?

keyIdea.title: Chain matters
keyIdea.text: chainId uniquely identifies a network; always verify chainId before interacting with contracts to prevent cross-chain mistakes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Networks & IDs
Common chainIds
Mainnet — chainId: 1
The production Ethereum network.
Sepolia — chainId: 11155111
A common testnet for contract testing and staging.
Local dev — chainId: 1337
Local networks (Ganache) or custom IDs for development.
Checking the chain
const currentChainHex = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_chainId' });
const currentChainId = parseInt(currentChainHex, 16);
if (currentChainId !== requiredChainId) {
  // prompt switch
}
Always parse the hex chainId when reading from the provider and compare to the numeric requiredChainId stored in configuration.
Key Takeaway

Treat chainId as authoritative for network checks; do not assume identical addresses across networks.

screens.title: Suggesting a network switch (wallet_switchEthereumChain)
screens.narratorSegment: To make it easier for users to connect to the network your contract requires, the provider exposes wallet_switchEthereumChain which can suggest a network change. Call window. ethereum. request with method wallet_switchEthereumChain and params containing the hexadecimal chainId of the desired network. If the user accepts, the chainChanged event will fire and your app can reinitialize accordingly. If the call fails, handle common error codes: 4001 means the user rejected the request, while 4902 indicates the target chain is not added to the user's wallet and must be added manually or via wallet_addEthereumChain if you supply configuration. Always catch these errors and provide clear, actionable messages rather than raw error objects. One helpful pattern is to first detect mismatch, display a concise modal that explains the required network and why it's needed, and then call wallet_switchEthereumChain on user confirmation. This avoids surprising pop-ups. Remember that programmatic switching is a suggestion to the wallet; the user retains full control. The key question: how will you guide users if their wallet does not support automatic addition of the required network? Suggesting a network switch (wallet_switchEthereumChain) means use wallet_switchethereumchain to request a network switch and handle errors like 4001 (rejection) and 4902 (network unknown).. In practical terms, programmatically suggest a chain switch and handle possible failures.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Suggested flow
Prompt user then call switch
Explain why you need the switch, then call wallet_switchEthereumChain to request it programmatically.
await window.ethereum.request({
  method: 'wallet_switchEthereumChain',

screens.title: Error handling and common error codes
screens.narratorSegment: Error handling is what separates a brittle DApp from a resilient one. The most frequently encountered error code is 4001, which indicates the user rejected a request such as eth_requestAccounts or a network switch. When this occurs, clear any pending state, inform the user why access is needed, and offer a simple retry path. Another common issue is a missing provider; if window. ethereum is absent, instruct the user to install MetaMask and offer a read-only fallback if your app supports it. For wallet_switchEthereumChain, a 4902 code means the requested network is not added to the user's wallet. In that case, you can suggest adding the network manually or use wallet_addEthereumChain if you can provide the required parameters. Always wrap provider calls in try/catch and avoid exposing raw error stacks in the UI. Log detailed errors to the console during development to debug, but present concise, actionable messages to users in production. A good pattern is to centralize provider interactions behind a small A P I layer that standardizes error messages, retries, and telemetry. Ask yourself: how will your app behave for each error type and will the user know the next step?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Error handling
Error codes
4001 — User rejected
Clear state and show a short explanation with a retry option.
4902 — Chain not found
Suggest manual add or use wallet_addEthereumChain if you can provide chain parameters.
Missing provider
Guide the user to install MetaMask and optionally provide a read-only fallback RPC.
Best practices
  • Wrap provider calls in try/catch and normalize errors in a single helper.
  • Provide clear user-facing messages and avoid raw error dumps.
  • Log details to the console or telemetry only during development or with consent.
Example handling
try {
  await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
} catch (err) {
  if (err.code === 4001) {
    // inform user and offer retry
  } else {
    // log and inform
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Standardize provider error handling, show concise user instructions, and avoid leaving the DApp in a broken state after rejections.

screens.title: Security best practices for wallet integration
screens.narratorSegment: Security in wallet integrations centers on the principle that the wallet manages secrets and signing; your DApp must never request or store private keys. MetaMask and other injected providers handle signing inside the extension, returning only public addresses and signed transaction data. Use provider methods and rely on the wallet's confirmation dialogs for user consent. Do not implement or request direct key import workflows unless you are building a wallet; instead use the provider APIs to sign and submit. Be careful with the information you display: never show sensitive details or reveal transaction payloads in a way that confuses the user. Validate user-entered addresses or parameters before sending them to the wallet to avoid mis-signed transactions. Finally, keep provider interactions asynchronous and handle race conditions that could lead to signing the wrong payload. For example, if a user switches accounts while a transaction is being built, ensure the transaction is rebuilt or canceled to prevent signing with a different account. The reflective question: how will you validate a transaction payload before sending it to the wallet for signing? Security best practices for wallet integration means never ask for private keys; use the provider for signing and ensure transaction payloads are validated before submission.. In practical terms, never ask for private keys and respect the wallet's signing model.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Security
Principles
  • Never request or store private keys in the DApp.
  • Always use provider signing flows for transactions and messages.
  • Validate all user inputs and transaction parameters before passing them to the wallet.
Practical checks
If a user changes account during transaction construction, cancel or rebuild the transaction to ensure the signer is correct.
Misconception
Thinking that obtaining the user's address grants you signing authority. Addresses are public; signing is always controlled by the wallet.
Key Takeaway

Trust the wallet for key management and signing. Validate payloads and handle account changes to avoid accidental signatures.

screens.title: Walkthrough: Connect to MetaMask and display account/network
screens.narratorSegment: This guided walkthrough mirrors the hands-on activity in the chapter. Start with a minimal H T M L page and a JavaScript file that references Web3. js. On load, check if window. ethereum exists and if the provider has already authorized accounts using eth_accounts. Populate the UI with the current connection status, account address, and network id. Provide a Connect action that calls eth_requestAccounts inside a try/catch block, stores the selected account on success, and initializes web3 with new Web3(window. ethereum). The starter code includes mapping network ids to friendly names so users can see where they are connected. A practical tip: during development, open the browser console to observe logged events so you can iterate quickly on listener behavior. After you implement this flow, ask: does the UI remain consistent when the user rejects or disconnects?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Hands-on Walkthrough
Starter HTML
<!-- index.html -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
  <title>MetaMask Connector</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Connect Your MetaMask Wallet</h1>
  <div id="status">Connection Status: Not Connected</div>
  <script src="app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
Starter JS
// app.js (outline)
let web3; let currentAccount = null;
async function connectWallet(){
  if (window.ethereum){
    try{
      const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
      currentAccount = accounts[0];
      web3 = new Web3(window.ethereum);
      // update UI and listeners
    } catch(err){ /* handle 4001 etc */ }
  } else { console.error('MetaMask not installed'); }
}
window.addEventListener('load', async ()=>{/* check eth_accounts */});
Key Takeaway

Follow the connect pattern, initialize web3 with window.ethereum, and set up listeners for dynamic wallet changes while testing thoroughly in the browser.

screens.title: Common mistakes and a troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: A short troubleshooting checklist helps you quickly identify integration errors during development and in production. First, verify provider detection: ensure window. ethereum exists and that you used the correct modern A P I rather than legacy window. web3. Second, confirm that eth_requestAccounts is awaited and that you handle code 4001 on rejection. Third, check that you read the chainId correctly (parse hex when using eth_chainId) and compare it to your requiredChainId. Fourth, ensure event listeners are registered once and not duplicated across hot reloads. Fifth, handle chainChanged by reinitializing contracts or reloading the page and treat empty accounts arrays as disconnects. Sixth, do not ask for private keys; rely on the wallet for signing. If a user reports stale account display after switching, the most likely cause is missing accountsChanged handling. If contract calls fail after a network switch, verify the chainId and re-create contract instances. During debugging always reproduce the issue with the wallet open and watch the console for emitted events. This checklist covers the common failure modes and gives you direct remediation steps so you can restore correct behavior quickly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1

First, an Injected Provider is the window. ethereum object that a browser wallet like MetaMask injects into the page; it is the gateway for signing and account access. Second, eth_requestAccounts is the JSON-RPC method used to prompt the user for permission and to return the array of authorized accounts when the user accepts. Third, accountsChanged is the event emitted when the user switches their selected account; handling it keeps your DApp in sync. These three items form the minimal vocabulary for connecting a DApp to a browser wallet. Memorize them as you build: detect the provider, ask for accounts, and subscribe to account events. Each term has practical code patterns and failure modes discussed earlier, so pair these definitions with the hands-on code examples to reinforce the behavior.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the exact techniques a user-facing DApp needs to connect to a browser wallet like MetaMask and maintain a reliable connection. You will learn how to detect the injected provider, request permission to access accounts, initialize Web3. js with that provider, and react to dynamic changes such as account switches and network switches. We will also review network identifiers like chainId, common network types you’ll encounter in development and testing, and best practices for error handling and security. This knowledge matters because user wallets mediate all signing operations; your DApp must never manage private keys directly. As a concrete example, we'll show the standard pattern using window. ethereum. request with eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user and then use web3. eth. net. getId to confirm the network. A common misconception is that once connected the environment is static — in reality users can switch accounts or networks any moment, so event listeners are essential. At the end you’ll be able to detect, connect, ask for the right network, and recover cleanly from user rejections or missing wallets. Think of this chapter as the bridge between your UI and the user’s wallet, and ask yourself: how will my app behave if the user changes networks right now?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to detect and connect to an injected Web3 provider in a browser environment, request account access from the user, and initialize Web3. js so that all blockchain requests route through the user's wallet. You will also be able to recognize and react to account and network changes by subscribing to accountsChanged and chainChanged events, keeping your DApp state synchronized with the user's wallet. Another objective is to distinguish between common network types—Mainnet, Sepolia, Goerli, and local development chains—by reading chainId values and enforcing a required chain before interacting with a deployed contract. Finally, you will implement robust error handling, including gracefully managing user rejections and network-mismatch scenarios. Each objective includes a short rationale and a mnemonic to make the skill easy to recall during development and debugging. These competencies matter because correct wallet integration prevents user confusion and avoids sending transactions on the wrong network or for the wrong account.

We will map the chapter objectives to a Bloom-style progression so you can track skill growth from learning to mastery. First, Learn: recognize window. ethereum, read provider properties, and identify the chainId. Second, Understand: explain why MetaMask injects a provider and how eth_requestAccounts prompts user permission. Third, Apply: write code that initializes Web3. js with window. ethereum, request accounts, and set up listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged. Fourth, Master: combine checks for requiredChainId, use wallet_switchEthereumChain to suggest a network switch, and implement resilient UI updates that recover from user rejections. Each stage includes a practical task: detection, prompting, listening, and network enforcement. This progression keeps focus on real developer tasks and helps you design tests that verify not only that code runs but that it behaves correctly when users change accounts or networks. A common misconception is equating networkId and chainId; treat chainId as the canonical identifier for chain comparisons in modern providers.

A robust DApp always checks for an injected provider before calling provider methods. The injected object is window. ethereum, and it follows the EIP‑1193 provider standard. Start by checking if window. ethereum exists and then use metadata such as isConnected or chainId to understand the current connection. If the provider is missing, guide the user to install a wallet. A common beginner mistake is to assume window. web3 will exist; modern providers expose window. ethereum and sometimes window. web3 for legacy compatibility, but relying on window. ethereum is the safer approach. For example, test for window. ethereum and display a friendly message that explains why the DApp needs permission. Remember that an absent provider is a user-flow issue, not a runtime bug — handle it with clear, non-technical text. Also be prepared for scenarios where a browser environment restricts extensions; for such cases, offer a fallback read-only RPC provider if appropriate. Finally, include telemetry or console logs for debugging during development, but never expose sensitive details to end users. Consider the sequence: detect provider, prompt install or continue, then request accounts. How will your DApp behave when the provider appears only after install?

Requesting account access is the step where the wallet asks the user for explicit permission to share account addresses with your DApp. The canonical method is to call window. ethereum. request with the method eth_requestAccounts. When accepted, the call returns an array of addresses with the user's primary account at index zero. When rejected, the provider throws an error with code 4001. Your DApp must handle both outcomes. A typical pattern is to await the request inside a try/catch, set the selectedAccount on success, and update the UI accordingly. On rejection clear any partial state and show a concise prompt explaining why the connection is required. Avoid repeatedly prompting the user; if the user rejects, provide guidance instead. The narration example below shows the common try/catch behavior and the recommended state updates. A common misconception is treating eth_accounts as identical to eth_requestAccounts — eth_accounts returns already-authorized accounts, whereas eth_requestAccounts actively prompts the user. Use eth_requestAccounts when you must obtain permission interactively. In practice test the flow by installing MetaMask, clicking connect, approving or rejecting, and verifying the DApp updates or cleans up state as appropriate. What feedback will you show the user on rejection?

After accounts are granted, initialize Web3. js using the injected provider so that all subsequent calls go through the user's wallet. The pattern is straightforward: web3 = new Web3(window. ethereum); this ensures transaction signing and account queries are routed correctly. Immediately after initialization you should retrieve the network id or chainId so your DApp knows which blockchain it's connected to. Use web3. eth. net. getId() for a numeric network id, or window. ethereum. request with eth_chainId to get the provider's chainId in hexadecimal — convert it to an integer when comparing to your requiredChainId. Initializing web3 ties together account, provider, and contract instances; if the user later changes networks, those contract instances may reference the wrong chain and should be recreated. A pitfall is caching contract objects without checking the current chain; always revalidate after a chainChanged event. As an example, once you call new Web3(window. ethereum), make a synchronous call to getId or request eth_chainId, verify it matches your expected value, and then proceed to instantiate contract wrappers. The closing question: what will you recreate or refresh when the chain changes?

Accounts can change at any time when the user switches accounts in their wallet. The provider emits accountsChanged with an array of addresses when that happens. Your DApp must subscribe to this event and update its internal selectedAccount and any UI that depends on it. Implementing window. ethereum. on('accountsChanged', handler) allows you to react immediately. In your handler, if newAccounts has length, set selectedAccount to newAccounts[0] and refresh any account-specific information like balances or nonces. If newAccounts is empty, the user has locked or disconnected their accounts — clear state and prompt the user to reconnect. A frequent error is to simply re-render without removing older listeners, which can cause duplicate handlers; ensure listeners are registered once or removed when appropriate. Also avoid forcing a full page reload on small account changes; a targeted UI refresh and state update is a cleaner UX. Example: after receiving the new account, call your data refresh routines and log the change for debugging. Consider: how will you surface a clear message to the user when their account is disconnected? Listening for accountsChanged events means listen to accountschanged, update selectedaccount, refresh account data, and handle empty arrays as a disconnect signal.. In practical terms, keep the dapp's selected account in sync with the wallet.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. When a user switches the active network in their wallet, the provider emits a chainChanged event with the new chainId in hexadecimal. This change can break contract interactions if your DApp remains configured for the previous network. The simplest reliable strategy is to reload or reinitialize network-dependent objects when chainChanged fires. Many developers use window. location. reload() inside the handler as a quick way to ensure every component is rebuilt for the new chain. Alternatively you can parse the new chainId, compare it to your requiredChainId, and then programmatically reinitialize Web3 and contract instances if it matches. If it does not match, present a clear prompt and optionally suggest wallet_switchEthereumChain. Be mindful of UX: reloading will lose local UI state, so communicate clearly if you choose that option. A common misconception is that chain changes only affect transactions — in fact they affect all chain-specific data including contract addresses and event logs. Decide whether to reload or rebuild in place based on how your app manages state, and always test the chainChanged flow by switching networks in your wallet. Ethereum networks are distinguished by numeric identifiers called chainId (and older networkId values). Knowing these is essential to avoid sending transactions to the wrong chain. The chapter lists common values you will encounter: Mainnet has chainId 1, Sepolia uses 11155111, Goerli commonly shows 5 though it is now deprecated in some flows, and local development networks like Ganache often use 1337 or a custom id. Use web3. eth. net. getId or window. ethereum. request with eth_chainId to read the current chain and compare it against the requiredChainId for your contract. A useful habit is to centralize requiredChainId in configuration so contract calls can check it before executing. A common mistake is assuming testnet and Mainnet share the same addresses — they do not. Contract addresses and state are chain-specific. For example, querying a contract address on Mainnet will return different data than the same address on Sepolia, and sometimes the address may not exist at all on another network. Always verify chainId programmatically before performing writes or reads that assume a specific deployment. How will your app prevent accidental mainnet transactions during testing?

Error handling is what separates a brittle DApp from a resilient one. The most frequently encountered error code is 4001, which indicates the user rejected a request such as eth_requestAccounts or a network switch. When this occurs, clear any pending state, inform the user why access is needed, and offer a simple retry path. Another common issue is a missing provider; if window. ethereum is absent, instruct the user to install MetaMask and offer a read-only fallback if your app supports it. For wallet_switchEthereumChain, a 4902 code means the requested network is not added to the user's wallet. In that case, you can suggest adding the network manually or use wallet_addEthereumChain if you can provide the required parameters. Always wrap provider calls in try/catch and avoid exposing raw error stacks in the UI. Log detailed errors to the console during development to debug, but present concise, actionable messages to users in production. A good pattern is to centralize provider interactions behind a small A P I layer that standardizes error messages, retries, and telemetry. Ask yourself: how will your app behave for each error type and will the user know the next step?

Security in wallet integrations centers on the principle that the wallet manages secrets and signing; your DApp must never request or store private keys. MetaMask and other injected providers handle signing inside the extension, returning only public addresses and signed transaction data. Use provider methods and rely on the wallet's confirmation dialogs for user consent. Do not implement or request direct key import workflows unless you are building a wallet; instead use the provider APIs to sign and submit. Be careful with the information you display: never show sensitive details or reveal transaction payloads in a way that confuses the user. Validate user-entered addresses or parameters before sending them to the wallet to avoid mis-signed transactions. Finally, keep provider interactions asynchronous and handle race conditions that could lead to signing the wrong payload. For example, if a user switches accounts while a transaction is being built, ensure the transaction is rebuilt or canceled to prevent signing with a different account. The reflective question: how will you validate a transaction payload before sending it to the wallet for signing? A short troubleshooting checklist helps you quickly identify integration errors during development and in production. First, verify provider detection: ensure window. ethereum exists and that you used the correct modern A P I rather than legacy window. web3. Second, confirm that eth_requestAccounts is awaited and that you handle code 4001 on rejection. Here are the core concepts you should remember. First, an Injected Provider is the window. ethereum object that a browser wallet like MetaMask injects into the page; it is the gateway for signing and account access. Second, eth_requestAccounts is the JSON-RPC method used to prompt the user for permission and to return the array of authorized accounts when the user accepts. Third, accountsChanged is the event emitted when the user switches their selected account; handling it keeps your DApp in sync. These three items form the minimal vocabulary for connecting a DApp to a browser wallet. Memorize them as you build: detect the provider, ask for accounts, and subscribe to account events. Each term has practical code patterns and failure modes discussed earlier, so pair these definitions with the hands-on code examples to reinforce the behavior.

A few additional essential concepts: chainChanged is the event emitted when the user changes networks; treat it as a context shift and reinitialize network-specific state. The chainId uniquely identifies an Ethereum network, for example 1 for Mainnet and 11155111 for Sepolia; always compare numeric values after parsing provider hex strings. Finally, EIP-1193 is the provider standard that defines how injected providers expose methods and events; modern wallets are EIP-1193-compliant, which is why you should prefer window. ethereum over legacy interfaces. Keep these items in mind while building: validate chainId before contract calls, handle chainChanged by rebuilding network-bound objects, and follow EIP-1193 patterns for requests and event subscriptions. These rules prevent cross-chain mistakes and ensure the UI matches the wallet state.
